Plus, proposed AI slowdown spooks tech sector
 

The hottest part of the global economy has been anything that played a supporting role in the great AI build-out. Calls to slow down the development of leading models for safety reasons, including an essay by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei over the weekend, have sent a chill through the tech sector. Mounting concerns about oil supplies, stoked by Saudi Arabia’s forced closure of a vital pipeline, aren’t helping the mood. U.S. stocks are likely to begin the week with losses.

A historic rough patch

 

Between war, rising yields and AI wiping out humanity, there’s plenty to keep investors up at night lately.

 

But we’re now in the thick of a period when angst tends to rise almost no matter what else is in the headlines. The run-up to U.S. midterm elections is historically among the worst times to own American stocks.

 

Between the beginning of July and a month before election day, the S&P 500 has posted a loss half of the time with an average return of negative 2.4% over the past 40 years. The good news? Once the electoral outcome starts to become clear, tension lifts. Stocks have tended to recover in the final four weeks before Election Day.

 

Once the votes are counted, the S&P 500 has put in some very good performances. Does it matter who wins?

 

Republicans currently enjoy a trifecta—control of both houses of Congress plus the White House. That has been hard to maintain with control lost in 1994, 2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022. The last time a party retained a lock on both the executive and legislative branches was during the Carter administration.

 

It’s commonly believed that a divided government is good for stocks because business thrives when Washington’s hands are tied. There is some truth to that: Midterm losses of one-party control have preceded a gain over the following six-months of 10.4% on average since 1970, according to analysts at BlackRock. 

 

Betting on Polymarket as of Friday put the chance of Republicans retaining the House of Representatives at just 12%. A Democratic sweep has even odds.

 

But changing your stock market exposure based on the likely election outcome is probably a bad idea. The average stock market performance for all six month periods following midterm elections since 1970 has been good, beating the divided government scenario alone.

 

Shunning what could suddenly be an out-of-favor industry also could be a mistake. During President Obama’s two terms, for example, the healthcare sector he campaigned on overhauling had an excellent annualized return of 14.2%.

 

And, despite Joe Biden’s green credentials, old-fashioned fossil-fuel companies were the best performers when he was in office. That was following their last place showing during President Trump’s first term at negative 16.4% annualized.

 

Energy stocks have done great so far during his current term. But that’s largely for a reason that’s hurting his party’s electoral prospects politically—a Middle East oil supply shock.

 

The bad news for President Trump is that there are less than two months to fix that before Election Day. The good news for investors is that, no matter the outcome, the historical pre-midterm rough patch is almost over.

Stocks I’m Watching

 

↘️ Nvidia, Intel, Marvell Technology: Chip stocks slid premarket after leaders of the biggest AI companies called to slow development of the technology, raising questions over chip demand. Overseas chip stocks sold off, including SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics in South Korea and ASML in the Netherlands.

 

↘️ Oracle: The company said over the weekend that co-founder Larry Ellison scrapped plans to sell up to $7.5 billion worth of his Oracle stake, a day after first disclosing the plans. No reason for the change was given. Shares fell 3.5% premarket Monday, swept up in the broader tech selloff.

 

↘️ SoftBank Group: Shares of the Japanese tech conglomerate fell more than 10% in Tokyo. A slowdown in AI development could hit SoftBank’s sprawling AI investments, including its stake in OpenAI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that the company likely wouldn’t go public this year because of safety concerns.

 

↗️ CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Workday: Shares of cybersecurity and other software companies rallied. Many of the shares have been under pressure this year as investors bet their businesses would be displaced by new AI models.

 

↗️ ExxonMobil and Chevron: The U.S. energy companies’ shares climbed alongside oil prices.

 

🔎 Dave and Buster’s is expected to report earnings after the closing bell.
